clinicalPearls: Troublesome symptoms or complications arising from reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus
The cardinal symptoms are heartburn and acid regurgitation, and there may be atypical or extra-oesophageal features such as chest pain, chronic cough or laryngeal symptoms
It is broadly divided into erosive oesophagitis and non-erosive reflux disease based on endoscopic findings
Typical uncomplicated symptoms are often managed empirically with lifestyle measures and acid suppression without initial endoscopy
Alarm features such as dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia warrant prompt endoscopy
Complications include peptic stricture, Barrett oesophagus and, rarely, oesophageal adenocarcinoma
reference.pathophysiology: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease results from excessive reflux of gastric contents across a dysfunctional anti-reflux barrier at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, a hypotensive sphincter, hiatus hernia and impaired oesophageal clearance allow acidic (and sometimes non-acidic) refluxate to contact the oesophageal mucosa. Prolonged acid exposure injures the mucosa, causing oesophagitis and, over time, metaplastic and stricturing changes, while symptoms also depend on mucosal sensitivity.
additionalInvestigations: Empirical trial of acid suppression for typical symptoms
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for alarm features or refractory symptoms
Ambulatory reflux (pH or pH-impedance) monitoring to confirm reflux and correlate symptoms
Biopsy to assess for Barrett oesophagus or eosinophilic oesophagitis
redFlags: New symptoms in an older patient or a suspicious mass
reference.prognosis: Most patients achieve good symptom control with lifestyle measures and acid suppression; a minority develop complications such as stricture or Barrett oesophagus that require ongoing surveillance or intervention.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to reflux without confirming it in refractory cases
Missing eosinophilic oesophagitis as a cause of reflux-like symptoms and dysphagia
Overlooking cardiac causes of chest pain
Ignoring alarm features that mandate endoscopy
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Institute lifestyle measures: weight reduction, head-of-bed elevation, avoidance of late meals and dietary triggers, and smoking cessation
Acid suppression with a proton-pump inhibitor is the pharmacological mainstay, with H2-receptor antagonists and alginate or antacid preparations as adjuncts or for milder disease
Arrange prompt upper GI endoscopy for alarm features such as dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia, or for refractory symptoms
Confirm reflux with ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring and assess motility with oesophageal manometry before considering surgery
Offer anti-reflux surgery such as fundoplication, or an endoscopic anti-reflux procedure, for refractory or regurgitation-predominant disease
Undertake endoscopic dilatation of peptic strictures and surveillance of Barrett oesophagus for dysplasia
Continue long-term acid suppression at the lowest effective dose for relapsing or complicated disease
